notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes for all 29 verses of Hebrews 12. The research tools hit their usage limit early, so the notes come from what I could read before that. That means the full Enduring Word commentary (up to v. 14 only), the excerpts that came back with my searches, and Wesley's complete notes. I couldn't open Gill, Ellicott or the Pulpit Commentary in full. Most of the older-commentator points below come from pages that collect many commentaries on a verse (StudyLight, Bible Hub).

**Gaps:**
- I found **no Catholic or Orthodox pages** (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The only early-church material comes second-hand: the Pulpit Commentary on the early Church Fathers' reading of v. 1, and Ligonier quoting Jerome on v. 14.
- I found **no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material**. The only "popular teaching" points are Guzik on blaming sin on demons (v. 1), Precept Austin on "let go and let God" (v. 4) and Rick Renner (v. 29).
- **Labels:** where I call someone "Arminian", "Calvinist", "Wesleyan/Methodist" or "Restoration Movement", that is StudyLight's own label for that commentator.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The "cloud" is a figure for a huge crowd: the faithful of ch. 11 and probably believers since. Guzik says this verse may hint that people in heaven watch earth but can't prove it. He leans toward a second reading: they are witnesses *to* us by their lives, like martyrs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - "Weights" are things that may not be sin but still slow the runner. "Endurance" is the patience that overcomes difficulties, not passive acceptance (Barclay, quoted by Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Wesley: the cloud is a great crowd "tending upward"; they bear witness to the power of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Calvin: the verse closes ch. 11 by calling us to imitate those saints. Gill: the witnesses (or "martyrs") bore testimony for God and will later witness for or against us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-1.html
- **Are they watching us? A real split:**
  - *Yes:* The Pulpit Commentary says the saints watch us with sympathy and that "the Fathers generally" read it this way. Benson pictures them looking on and applauding. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-1.html
  - *No:* Constable says they are witnesses because they testified, not because they watch us now. Chuck Smith says the verse does not mean a gallery of saints watching. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-1.html
  - *No:* Piper notes that the verb "witness" in ch. 11 always means giving testimony, not spectating. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/running-with-the-witnesses
- **"The sin that entangles":** The Biblical Illustrator says it means sin in general, not one pet sin. Precept Austin's collection includes the opposite view: most people have one favourite sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-1.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_121
- **Popular teaching:** Guzik says Scripture gives no reason to blame our besetting sins on demons. The call is simply to lay sin aside in the Spirit's power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
- **Is salvation at stake in the race?**
  - Precept Austin: this race is "categorically not" a race for salvation; rewards can be lost, but not salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_121
  - Piper (quoted on the same page): the whole book warns us not to take our eternal security for granted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_121

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - "Looking" means looking *away* from everything else to Jesus (Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik). Guzik warns against treating Jesus as *only* an example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - "Author and finisher" echoes Phil 1:6: He starts our faith and finishes it. Jesus did not see the cross as joy; He looked past it to the joy beyond. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Wesley: Christ begins faith in us, carries it on and perfects it. Our looking to Him is like Israel looking at the bronze serpent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Pink: His "sitting down" means rest after finished work, rule, and the right to judge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_122
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - The NET translates "pioneer and perfecter" and notes an allusion to Ps 110:1. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=heb&chapter=12&verse=2
  - Utley: the verb means looking intently and continually; it may also picture keeping our focus on the new covenant. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
  - The Biblical Illustrator notes that here Christ's sufferings illustrate endurance, not their saving power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-1.html

**v. 3**
- Wesley: compare yourself with Him; if the Lord bore all this, shall His servants bear nothing? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Matthew Henry: Christ's sufferings far outweigh ours, so His patience is our pattern. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_012.cfm
- Barclay: "weary" and "lose heart" are words Aristotle used of a runner collapsing after the finish. The point is: don't collapse before the line. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/hebrews-12.html
- Guzik lists the hostility Jesus faced, from Nazareth to the cry "Crucify Him!" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/

**v. 4**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The readers faced social and economic persecution but not yet bloodshed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Barnes: they had not yet faced the severest test, so they should not give up. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
  - Wesley: "unto blood" means to wounds and death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Henry: "resist to blood" means sealing one's testimony with one's own blood, not shedding the enemy's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_012.cfm
- Moffatt (quoted by Precept Austin): the writer is shaming the readers, not blaming them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_123-4
- **Popular teaching:** Precept Austin says this verse rules out the "let go and let God" idea that any effort is the flesh. Believers must actively resist and strive. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_123-4
- Utley names two possible "sins" in view: unbelief (for unbelieving Jews) and apostasy, i.e. "shrinking back" (for believing Jews). https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12

**vv. 5–6**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The quotation from Prov 3:11–12 shows that discipline is a sign of sonship, not rejection. Discipline isn't the only reason for hardship; 2 Cor 1 gives another. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Wesley: don't put affliction down to chance; see God's hand in it. Everything springs from love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Utley: the word "forgotten" (used only here in the NT) may mean forgetting completely or deliberately. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
  - Precept Austin: discipline means "child-training", never punitive wrath, since Christ bore that. God governs even the hostility of sinners for His children's good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_125-6 ; http://preceptaustin.org/hebrews_125-6.htm
- **A difference of emphasis:**
  - Guzik: God chastens "without anger", only from love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Henry: afflictions "may be the fruits of God's displeasure" yet still prove fatherly love; even God's best children have faults that need correcting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_012.cfm

**v. 7**
- Wesley: a father chastens his son "when he offends". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Barnes: God has not cast you off. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
- Wuest (quoted by Precept Austin): the letter is written to a professing church that includes both saved and unsaved people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_127-10

**v. 8**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: people who think they're beyond correction class themselves with the illegitimate. When God lets sin pass uncorrected, that shows His wrath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - Wesley: all sons share in discipline, "more or less". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Utley: the grammar assumes that all God's children experience discipline. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
- **Disputed:**
  - Precept Austin warns against Zane Hodges's "questionable" reading of "illegitimate" in the Bible Knowledge Commentary. I only saw the warning, not Hodges's actual view. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_127-10
  - The same page quotes Don Anderson: people who escape the rod should ask whether they are truly born again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_127-10

**v. 9**
- Guzik: resenting God's correction treats Him as an equal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
- **A real difference on "Father of spirits":**
  - Wesley wonders whether it means our earthly fathers parent only our bodies, while God creates every soul directly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Utley says the phrase has nothing to do with theories of where the soul comes from; it means God is the source of all life. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the Creator and life-giver of all spirits. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/hebrews-12.html

**v. 10**
- Wesley: earthly fathers often go wrong through too much indulgence or too much severity. God always acts for our profit, so we share "himself and his glorious image". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Guzik: God knows everything, so He disciplines perfectly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: discipline has to hurt to work, and the fruit comes "afterward". Jesus is never given as an example in this section because He never needed correcting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
- Wesley: the fruit is holiness and happiness for those who accept the training as from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Barnes: faith doesn't make a Christian a stoic; it can make him feel suffering more. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
- De Haan (quoted by Precept Austin) takes "afterward" to mean after the race is over. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1211

**vv. 12–13**
- The NET notes quotations from Isa 35:3 and Prov 4:26. It explains "straight paths" as "stay on God's paths". https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Heb+12%3A12%2C13
- Wesley: lift up the hands, your own or your brothers'; remove every stumbling block for the weak. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Utley: "put out of joint" may echo 1 Kgs 18:21, where Israel wavered between two opinions. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
- Sproul (quoted by Precept Austin): "run tough together", since v. 13 is about the whole community. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1212-13

**v. 14**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: be right with people (peace) and with God (holiness). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/
  - The NET notes the link to "His holiness" in v. 10. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=heb&chapter=12&verse=14
- **Different emphases:**
  - Wesley (Wesleyan/Methodist): failing to pursue *all* holiness is "the direct way" into every kind of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Ligonier (Reformed): we must strive for holiness. It also quotes Jerome: "Christ is that sanctification" without which none see God. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-need-of-peace-and-holiness
  - Precept Austin: practical holiness is evidence of real faith. Without at least a longing for it, question whether your faith is genuine. "See the Lord" includes close fellowship now. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1214-17

**v. 15**
- This is the clearest split between traditions.
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The background is Deut 29:18: one idolater or apostate poisoning the community. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-15.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
  - Wesley: bitterness means envy, anger or suspicion. Any corruption of doctrine or practice can defile many. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Barclay: Theophylact pictured travellers checking that no one has fallen behind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** it is easy to fall from grace, so we must be vigilant to persevere. But it does not follow that grace only works if we cooperate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Calvinist Baptist (Gill):** this cannot mean God's unchangeable love or the grace planted in a believer's heart, which never fails. It means the gospel teaching about grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Matthew Henry:** apostasy means falling short of *true* grace despite outward religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Arminian / Restoration Movement:**
  - Coffman: grace offered to everyone can still fail in those who don't keep its conditions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
  - "Contending for the Faith" says the verse disproves the idea that you cannot fall from grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
  - Gann: the Greek suggests "falling back", which implies grace had been reached. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Cautious middle:**
  - One older commentator collected on Bible Hub says the verse should not be used in the falling-from-grace debate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-15.htm
  - Constable: the warning concerns believers who are failing; it should not be made a general statement of the plan of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html
- **Precept Austin:** the "root" is an obvious unbeliever posing as a believer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1214-17

**v. 16**
- Wesley: Esau was "profane" for despising the blessing that came with the birthright. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Barnes: sexual immorality is a sin that spreads corruption in the church. Esau threw away his highest honour for a trifle. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
- Henry: apostates are like Esau, giving up their inheritance to avoid persecution or for comfort. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/12-15.html

**v. 17**
- **"No place for repentance" in whom?**
  - *In Isaac:* Esau couldn't change his father's mind. This is held by the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, Meyer and JFB (taking "repentance" for the change Esau wanted in his father). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/hebrews-12.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-17.htm
  - *In the situation:* there was no chance to undo what he had done. This is held by Vincent, by Calvin (cited by Meyer), by Maclaren (who puts the clause in brackets: Esau sought the blessing, not repentance) and by Wesley. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-17.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hebrews/esaus-vain-tears.cfm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - *In Esau's heart:* repentance could no longer be stirred up in him. This is Bengel's view, cited by Meyer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-17.htm
- **Pastoral point:**
  - Maclaren: the verse does *not* teach that someone can want to repent with tears and be unable to. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hebrews/esaus-vain-tears.cfm
  - The Geneva notes say Esau's threat to kill Jacob shows what his "repentance" was worth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/12-17.htm
  - Precept Austin and Bible Hub: Esau's sorrow was about what he lost, not about sin; regret is not repentance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1214-17 ; https://biblehub.com/hebrews/12-17.htm

**vv. 18–21**
- Wesley: Sinai was an earthly, material mountain. The trumpet was sounded by angels before the Ten Commandments. Moses stood among the hearers and trembled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Utley: the people's terror recalls Exod 20:19 and Deut 5. The animal ban (Exod 19:12–13) shows God's awesome holiness. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
- Henry: the point is to keep the readers from slipping back into Judaism. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_012.cfm

**v. 22**
- Wesley: Zion is a spiritual mountain, and these titles belong to the New Testament church. The verse is about fellowship with the church in heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Precept Austin: "you have come" is perfect tense, so believers are already citizens. It describes salvation already gained, not only a future hope. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1222-24
- Guzik: at Sinai only Moses could come near; at Zion an "innumerable company" is invited. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/

**v. 23**
- Wesley:
  - "Church" means all true believers, on earth or in paradise. The firstborn are placed nearer God than the angels.
  - The "spirits of just men" are separated souls, probably New Testament believers, made perfect in a higher sense than the living.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Utley: the grammar means "made perfect by God", with lasting results. Because of 11:40 it may mean the Old Testament saints. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
- Guzik: Jesus' work satisfies God as Judge and so produces these "just men made perfect". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-12/

**v. 24**
- Wesley and Utley: Abel's blood cried for vengeance; Jesus' blood speaks mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12
- An academic study quoted by Precept Austin argues for a double meaning: Abel's murder, and also his acceptable sacrifice (11:4). https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1222-24

**v. 25**
- Wesley: to "refuse" Him is unbelief; the one speaking from heaven came from heaven to speak to us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- Utley: this is one of the book's two main warnings. Knowing the truth and not acting on it is dangerous for believers and unbelievers alike. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12

**vv. 26–27**
- **What is being shaken?**
  - Wesley: in a lower sense the end of the Jewish church and state; in full, the end of all things. The shaking began at Christ's first coming and ends at His second. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - Barnes: the coming of the gospel was weightier than the giving of the Law. Religious ideas not founded on truth will be removed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
  - Henry: the gospel kingdom will never give way to another dispensation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_012.cfm
  - Utley: Haggai 2:6 is quoted from the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), and it is about a new temple. He expects the world to be remade without the curse. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-12

**v. 28**
- Wesley: "let us have grace" means hold fast the grace. "Reverence" literally means shame, from a sense of our unworthiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
- The NET translates "let us give thanks". https://biblehub.com/net/hebrews/12.htm
- Piper: unlike Esau, be thankful and worship with awe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1227-29

**v. 29**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Barnes: the quotation is from Deut 4:24. There is as much reason to fear God's displeasure under the new covenant as under the old. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-12.html
  - Wesley: the fire is the strictness of God's justice and the purity of His holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-12.html
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: a human-style image of God's hatred of apostasy, not a description of God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/hebrews-12.html
  - Barclay: the God who could be your salvation becomes destroying fire to those who are false to Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/hebrews-12.html
- **Charismatic angle:** Rick Renner reads the fire as testing that clears the way for the Holy Spirit to transform us and set us ablaze. On the same page, Girdwood and another writer apply it to judgment on those who reject God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1227-29
